title: Buffett 1979 letter: ROE over EPS, inflation's misery index, and why turnarounds seldom turn
summary: Buffett argues managers should be judged on return on equity capital rather than EPS growth, shows how inflation plus taxes can erase even a 20% return, and explains why a good business at a fair price beats a poor one at a bargain. He also covers underwriting discipline, avoiding long bonds, and candid owner reporting.

principles.text: Judge management by return on equity capital without undue leverage, not by steady EPS growth.
principles.quote: The primary test of managerial economic performance is the achievement of a high earnings rate on equity capital employed (without undue leverage, accounting gimmickry, etc.) and not the achievement of consistent gains in earnings per share.

principles.text: Rising EPS can be an illusion: retained earnings alone make a stopped clock look like a growth stock.
principles.quote: Thus, even a “stopped clock” can look like a growth stock if the dividend payout ratio is low.

principles.text: Turnarounds seldom turn; a good business at a fair price beats a poor business at a bargain price.
principles.quote: “turnarounds” seldom turn, and that the same energies and talent are much better employed in a good business purchased at a fair price than in a poor business purchased at a bargain price.

principles.text: Inflation plus the tax cost of cashing out can exceed a business's return, shrinking real capital.
principles.quote: When this index exceeds the rate of return earned on equity by the business, the investor’s purchasing power (real capital) shrinks even though he consumes nothing at all.

principles.text: Don't lock in a fixed price on money for decades in an inflationary world; avoid very long bonds.
principles.quote: our unwillingness to fix a price now for a pound of See’s candy or a yard of Berkshire cloth to be delivered in 2010 or 2020 makes us equally unwilling to buy bonds which set a price on money now for use in those years.

principles.text: Underwrite only business that makes sense, even if volume falls; don't lay off people over it.
principles.quote: if business makes sense, he writes it; if it doesn’t, he rejects it.
